strong_form: People with a learning-disability label are over-represented among the most intellectually accomplished people (top achievers in science, art, business) compared with their population base rate.
weak_form: Some LD subgroups (e.g. dyslexia among entrepreneurs) are over-represented in specific high-achievement niches, and the label can mask high ability (twice-exceptional).
refuted_if: Representative samples of top achievers show LD rates at or below the population base rate, or LD-labeled cohorts show lower average and lower top-percentile attainment.

prior_art.citation: Logan, 'Dyslexic entrepreneurs: the incidence; their coping strategies and their business skills', Dyslexia 2009 (35% of US entrepreneurs self-report dyslexia vs 1% of corporate managers)
NPR, 'Does Dyslexia Translate to Business Success?' (2007)
Eloranta 2019, Finnish longitudinal dissertation: childhood LD linked to lower educational attainment and more unemployment
Conti-Ramsden et al. 2018, JSLHR: developmental language disorder linked to lower qualifications
Adults with Learning Disabilities 8-15 Years after College (no difference in degree completion among college grads)

strongest_criticism: Longitudinal cohorts show that LD-labeled people on average reach lower educational attainment and higher unemployment, so the general claim fails. The best supporting evidence is a small self-report survey of entrepreneurs, which is one niche and is open to selection effects (dyslexic people pushed out of credentialed careers into self-employment), so it says nothing about intellectual accomplishment in general. Lists of famous 'LD geniuses' are anecdotal and often rest on retrospective diagnosis.
